identity.title: Focal deficit screen: facial droop, arm drift, speech (Cincinnati/NIHSS-lite)

technique.how: Brief structured screen: facial symmetry on smile, pronator drift with arms held out and eyes closed for 10 s, and speech (repeat a sentence, name objects). Add gaze (ask to look left/right), visual fields by confrontation, finger-nose and heel-shin, and gait if safe, because dizzy or confused patients often lack the three classic items.
technique.prerequisites: Bedside glucose; note baseline deficits, time last known well and anticoagulant use. Patient must be able to follow at least one-step commands or the screen defaults to observation of asymmetry.
technique.contraindications: None. Do not stand a patient who is vomiting, severely ataxic or hypotensive to test gait.

interpretation.positive_finding: Any new focal finding (facial paresis, arm drift, dysarthria/aphasia, gaze palsy, hemisensory loss, limb ataxia) strongly favours a central lesion; in dizzy patients such general neurologic signs are highly specific for a central cause (pooled specificity about 93%; limb weakness 98.5%).
interpretation.negative_finding: A normal focal screen lowers stroke probability modestly overall (LR about 0.4 for absence of face/arm/speech findings) but is insensitive for posterior-circulation stroke: pooled sensitivity of the general neurologic exam in acute vertigo is under 50%, and in Kattah's AVS cohort general signs were absent in 49% of central lesions.
interpretation.pitfalls: Confusion, aphasia and encephalopathy from hypoglycemia, seizure or intoxication mimic focal deficits; a normal screen in a dizzy patient is falsely reassuring, so add HINTS and a gait test. Old deficits must be compared with baseline.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: treat as stroke until imaged, especially if anticoagulated (urgent CT for hemorrhage). Negative in a dizzy patient: still needs HINTS/gait assessment; does not exclude stroke.

estimates.population: Pooled studies of patients with neurologically relevant symptoms, modern neuroimaging (RCE systematic review)
estimates.reference_standard: Final diagnosis after neuroimaging and laboratory tests
estimates.quote: acute facial paresis, arm drift, or abnormal speech increases the likelihood of stroke (LR of > or =1 finding = 5.5; 95% CI, 3.3-9.1)

estimates.target_condition: Central cause (stroke, hemorrhage, other) of acute vertigo/dizziness - general neurologic examination abnormal
estimates.population: ED patients with acute vertigo or dizziness; 5 studies, 869 patients
estimates.quote: general neurologic examination-five studies, 869 patients, pooled sensitivity 46.8% (95% confidence interval [CI] 32.3%-61.9%, moderate certainty) and specificity 92.8% (95% CI 75.7%-98.1%

estimates.target_condition: Central cause of acute vertigo/dizziness - limb weakness/hemiparesis
estimates.population: ED patients with acute vertigo or dizziness; 4 studies, 893 patients
estimates.quote: limb weakness/hemiparesis-four studies, 893 patients, sensitivity 11.4% (95% CI 5.1%-23.6%, high) and specificity 98.5% (95% CI 97.1%-99.2%, high)

estimates.target_condition: Central acute vestibular syndrome (stroke or other central lesion) - any general neurologic sign including truncal ataxia
estimates.population: 101 consecutive high-risk AVS patients (25 peripheral, 76 central) at a stroke referral center
estimates.reference_standard: MRI (or CT) for stroke; normal MRI plus clinical follow-up for peripheral
estimates.location: Table 1 (PAVS n=25 vs CAVS n=76), Stroke 2009;40:3504 (PMC4593511)

sources.citation: Goldstein LB, Simel DL. Is this patient having a stroke? JAMA. 2005;293(19):2391-2402.

Diagnostic accuracy of the physical examination in emergency department patients with acute vertigo or dizziness: a systematic review and meta-analysis for GRACE-3. Acad Emerg Med. 2023;30(5):552-578.

Kattah JC, Talkad AV, Wang DZ, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. HINTS to diagnose stroke in the acute vestibular syndrome: three-step bedside oculomotor examination more sensitive than early MRI diffusion-weighted imaging. Stroke. 2009;40(11):3504-3510.
Kothari RU, Pancioli A, Liu T, Brott T, Broderick J. Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale: reproducibility and validity. Ann Emerg Med. 1999;33(4):373-378.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Never use a normal three-item screen to exclude stroke in acute vertigo, ataxia, diplopia or visual loss; posterior-circulation strokes frequently have none of the three findings.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: New focal deficit in an anticoagulated patient is intracranial hemorrhage until proven otherwise: urgent CT and reversal pathway. Any focal deficit within the reperfusion window is time-critical.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Item reliability varies from slight to almost perfect (Goldstein 2005); structured scoring (NIHSS/CPSS) improves agreement; CPSS items ICC 0.75-0.91 across paramedics and physicians (Kothari 1999).

extraction_notes: This record overlaps exam_face_arm_speech_cpss; it adds the pooled accuracy of a broader general neurologic examination in dizzy ED patients (GRACE-3 meta-analysis, abstract) and Kattah 2009 Table 1 (PMC full text). Kattah 2009 sensitivity/specificity are read directly from the Table 1 percentages (0% of peripheral vs 51% of central had general signs) with the table's reported NLR; specificity 100% derives from 0/25 peripheral patients. GRACE-3 setting is ED; population includes all acute vertigo/dizziness, not only AVS. Goldstein pooled LRs are from the abstract because the JAMA tables were not accessible.
